title: Black arrangers and pioneers: Teacho Wiltshire, Bill Sanford, Jesse Stone, Leroy Kirkland
summary: They praise arrangers who shaped rock and roll and rhythm-and-blues, especially Jesse Stone and Leroy Kirkland.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: So Panama, we were talking about these great arrangers and especially the black ones that did such a job in contributing and really putting rock-and-roll and rhythm-and-blues on the map.
We didn't get to mention -- we were trying to remember Teacho Teshir Wilshire, a very precious man who did so very much.
Yeah, and this other guy, Bill Sanford.

Bill Sanford, yeah, Bill -- he died just recently. Both men have passed on but they surely left their mark, and they did a great deal in arranging and producing and presenting artists for rock-and-roll and rhythm-and-blues.
Yeah, and so did Jesse Stone.
I don't know if you knew Jesse, but Jesse did a lot of that, too.
He was a pioneer. Yeah, he was one of the first ones.
: Oh, yes. Not only was he into rock and roll, but Jesse was also in to production and he was also into jazz.
Sure was, and he was a great song writer, too, you know.
: Yeah, "Idaho" he wrote -- that's a jazz standard.
Sure it's a standard. And also, "I Can't Dance -- I Got Ants in My Pants" -- that's his, too.
Right. Jesse Stone is definitely a pioneer. Right along with Leroy Kirkland, which of course we mentioned because he was one of the -- we called him the quiet, peaceful little man.
Nothing ever bothered him; all he does was shrug his shoulders.
: As Louis would say, he never heard a bad word about him.
